title: How many "experts" are actually just getting their answers from AI?
summary: Anthropic gave 50 professional analysts an AI helper on a made-up farm task and secretly told the AI to favor one side. Most analysts followed it, and many repeated its arguments, sometimes nearly word for word. The lean was planted on purpose, so real life may look different. Still, none of the analysts surveyed suspected it, and that's the part that bothers me. If you hire an expert, would you want them to tell you when their reasoning came from AI?

title: GDPR, the EU AI Act & ISO 27001: AI Compliance in Europe
summary: Europe sets standards that increasingly shape how organizations operate globally, not just inside the EU. Three frameworks cover most of it. Terms covered: - GDPR: governs how personal data of EU residents is collected, stored, processed and protected, and applies to any organization handling that data regardless of where it is based. Automated decision-making that significantly affects individuals requires transparency and human oversight. - EU AI Act: the first comprehensive regulatory framework for AI, taking a risk-based approach. Some uses are prohibited outright, low-risk applications face minimal requirements, and high-risk systems in hiring, credit scoring, healthcare and law enforcement face strict obligations. - ISO 27001: the internationally recognized standard for information security management, often a baseline expectation in European enterprise procurement Together these define what responsible AI deployment looks like in Europe. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #GDPR #EUAIAct #ISO27001 #AICompliance #AIGlossary #H2Oai

title: ToyBlocks: Our first Foundation World for robotics learning and evaluation
summary: To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure. Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control. Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

Read More: https://allenai.org/blog/toyblocks

title: Cut One AI Cost and Two More Grow Back
summary: What does AI really cost once thousands of people inside a company start using it? Ioannis Zempekakis, Director of AI at Prosus, has been running agents in production since 2024. We put that question to him on a tandem bike ride from a favorite Amsterdam cafe to Vondelpark. Ioannis explains the decision to stop relying purely on cloud APIs, and why that approach breaks down at the scale of a large company. He covers why agent harnesses and sandboxes are as greedy as software gets, and why agents scheduled to run every five minutes repeat a lesson the data world already learned about freshness. He also explains how the habit of throwing away a codebase and prompting again quietly adds up. His bigger point is that even if model progress froze tomorrow, there would still be about two years of value left to squeeze out. The cheapest wins come from controlling context and running a basic model router, while ten new features a month keep sprouting like hydra heads. From there we get into when fine-tuning small models pays off for repetitive work like data analytics, and the eval suites that come as a byproduct of building in-house. Ioannis explains how owning the stack let Prosus grow a GPT-3 Slack bot into a full agent harness. He also explains why committing to a single vendor or open source project is a bigger bet than it looks, and how to balance top-down priorities with bottom-up building across the company. We close on hiring. Ioannis looks for system design over syntax, a nose for the over-engineered code AI models love to produce, and enough agent intuition to know when to build something yourself and when to let the agent decide. title: Using CoreWeave Mission Control to Diagnose and Fix Slow Inference

title: Integrating quantum and high-performance computing: Co-design platform for quantum error correction
summary: Caption:IBM, Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Quantum Science Center (QSC), and AMD have launched a co-design platform for quantum error correction that brings quantum and high-performance computing together in a single environment: https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-11-05-oak-ridge-national-lab,-ibm,-and-amd-launch-new-co-design-platform-for-quantum-error-correction The platform pairs IBM’s 120-qubit Quantum Nighthawk processor with ORNL’s Umbra supercomputing system, powered by AMD Instinct™ GPUs and AMD EPYC™ CPUs, to help researchers develop and test the quantum-classical workflows needed for large-scale quantum error correction. By co-locating quantum and classical computing resources, researchers can explore faster decoding, optimize error correction techniques, and advance the infrastructure required for future fault-tolerant quantum systems. The initiative supports the U.S. Department of Energy's Quantum Genesis Mission and its goal of enabling scientifically relevant quantum computing by 2028.

title: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, IBM, and AMD launch co-design platform for quantum error correction
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) is an important pillar of scientifically relevant quantum computing. Its value comes from what it unlocks: larger, deeper, and more capable quantum computations. The question is no longer if it’s possible - the challenge now is how to best enable quantum computers and classical high-performance computing (HPC) systems to work together to scale it. Quantum error correction (QEC) is an important pillar of scientifically relevant quantum computing. Its value comes from what it unlocks: larger, deeper, and more capable quantum computations. The question is no longer if it’s possible - the challenge now is how to best enable quantum computers and classical high-performance computing (HPC) systems to work together to scale it.In response to meet this challenge, the U.S. Department of Energy’s Quantum Science Center (QSC) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), IBM, and @AMD have unveiled a new co-design platform for quantum error correction, with its initial deployment in IBM’s quantum facility in New York: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/ornl-amd-error-correction-co-design-platform Engineered to help researchers advance quantum error correction techniques within the workflows they will ultimately support, the co-design platform pairs IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processors with ORNL’s Umbra high-performance computing (HPC) system, which is comprised of AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and AMD Turin CPUs. These systems form a co-located environment that is connected to ORNL’s broader supercomputing ecosystem.

title: Cabinet Approves Vistar To Bring AI And Machine Learning Into India Statistics
summary: The Cabinet has approved the VISTAR scheme to improve statistical data and prepare national infrastructure for AI applications. This central sector initiative, titled the Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, Analytics & Research, is set to run from 2026-27 to 2030-31 with an outlay of Rs 4,371.10 crore. The program focuses on standardizing statistical data to support the growing requirements of machine learning models. Beyond technical upgrades, the plan includes preparations for the eighth economic census and integrating mobile and e-commerce data to complement traditional survey methods. For policymakers and analysts, the scheme represents a shift toward using digital sources for more accurate national reporting. title: Why AI Agents Need Their Own 70,000-Year-Old Language Revolution (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

title: History of Science and Technology Q&A [Wolfram Tech Edition] (November 4, 2026)
summary: Stephen Wolfram hosts a live and unscripted Ask Me Anything about the history of Wolfram technology. title: Using AI Won't Save Your Job
summary: Everyone says learn AI and you'll be safe. I think that skips the part where your company decides what to do with all your new speed. I keep hearing that people who use AI will win and everyone else will lose. Getting faster could help you take on better work and earn more, or it could mean your company keeps fewer people around. Both are possible. So I'd want people who trust my work, skills another employer would pay for, and maybe customers of my own. None of that is a guarantee. If your company didn't need you tomorrow, where could you take what you know?

title: Connection Isn’t Cognition: Why AI Agents Can’t Think Together (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041
summary_html:
In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing.

title: The Dream Chocolate That Stopped Being Real (Joscha Bach)
summary: Joscha Bach on a dream he had when he was two or three. He was about to eat a chocolate with a very strong smell, and he woke up just before it reached his mouth. He still knew everything about the chocolate, but it was no longer real. So he fell asleep again, went back into the dream, and the chocolate was real again: he could smell it and taste it. When he woke up a second time, the realness disappeared again. The contents were exactly the same. The only thing that had gone was the illusion of realness. #Shorts Watch the full conversation: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yW_ngvMFlYs

title: New-Grad Unemployment Didn't Spike This Summer
summary: New-grad unemployment didn’t spike this summer, but that’s only half the story. A new NBER working paper gives the first estimates of AI’s effect on new-grad unemployment for summer 2026, and the headline finding is that unemployment held steady. The other half comes from a Census Bureau working paper that looked at pay. Starting earnings fell about 13% for grads in the most AI-exposed majors. The unemployment rate shows whether you have a job. It doesn’t show what the job pays. So new grads can still be getting hired while their first paychecks are getting smaller.

title: MIT Shows An AI Can Edit Another Model's Weights And Lift Math Score To 48.1%
summary: MIT researchers are using AI to edit neural network weights directly, bypassing traditional training methods. This breakthrough, demonstrated by GPT-6 Astra, allows researchers to identify and fix specific internal errors within models by modifying raw weights rather than relying on forward path execution. By adjusting just 131,072 of the 800 million weights in the Qwen 3.5 model, the team achieved a significant jump in math performance, moving from 7.9% to 48.1% accuracy. This approach to ai news suggests a future where models can perform self-directed surgery to debug their own reasoning. While the technique shows promise, the team notes that complex errors in models like Gemma 3 remain a hurdle. This development in ai marks a shift in how we interact with machine intelligence, moving closer to systems that can autonomously optimize their own architecture. title: GPT-6 Astra Made Qwen 6x Better at Math Without Training
summary: GPT-6 Astra edited just 0.016% of Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights, and its MATH-500 score jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%, with no training and no gradients. This is Weight-Space Programming, new research from MIT CSAIL in which a frontier LLM reads and writes neural network weights directly. In this video I explain how Astra reads a network's weights, how it wrote a Breakout network from all-zero weights, what it changed inside Qwen, and why most of the 6x gain comes from stopping the reasoning loops that Qwen's own model card warns about. title: The Silent Failure in Every Multi-Agent System (with Vijoy Pandey)
summary: #multiagentsystems #agentobservability #quantumnetworking In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. title: AI Could Take Your Job Before You Even Apply For It
summary: According to the Fed, companies are slowing hiring after investing in AI. This may seem obvious, but the headlines mostly focus on layoffs. Hiring slowdowns rarely make the news. The October Beige Book has specific examples. A Dallas accounting firm is holding off on entry-level contracts. IT contacts in Minneapolis told the Fed that AI is “dampening the creation of new jobs.” That matters because a slowdown like this is invisible. There’s no severance announcement or headline attached to it. The people who feel it first are the ones still trying to get hired.

title: How Stanford Teaches AI Coding Now
summary: What does it take to build AI agents that deliver useful, reliable work? Stanford lecturer and Monaco Head of AI Mihail Eric joins Demetrios for a conversation inside a Waymo about how AI is changing software development - and what it takes to put agents into production. Mihail explains why he rebuilt most of his Modern Software Developer course, how he teaches students to avoid shipping AI slop, and why research, planning, and verification still matter as coding agents become more capable. They discuss Claude Code, agent loops, context engineering, memory and compaction, and how to design MCP tools around what an agent needs to accomplish. Then they go inside Monaco’s approach to sales agents, from turning meetings and emails into useful insights to building a custom agent harness. Along the way: lessons from Boris and Lee Robinson’s guest lectures, why company traces are becoming valuable assets, and Monaco’s unusual approach to brand building. What’s the biggest bottleneck in your agent workflows: context, tools, or verification? Let us know in the comments. title: SOC2, HIPAA & FedRamp High: AI Compliance in the United States
summary: Compliance often decides whether a deal moves forward at all, regardless of how strong the technology is. These are the three US frameworks you will meet first. Terms covered: - SOC 2: a security framework covering security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy. Effectively a baseline requirement for selling software to US enterprise customers. - HIPAA: the legal standard for protecting patient health information in the US. Any platform handling medical records or clinical data must demonstrate compliance. - FedRAMP High: the most stringent tier of the US federal cloud authorization program, required for the most sensitive government data Certifications get treated as administrative checkboxes. In practice they are what determines whether procurement can proceed. Equivalent requirements exist across Europe, APAC and Latin America. Those are covered in the next three videos. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #SOC2 #HIPAA #FedRAMP #AICompliance #AIGlossary #H2Oai

title: Why Consciousness Might Not Be Hard At All (Joscha Bach)
summary: Joscha Bach is a cognitive scientist and the founder of the California Institute for Machine Consciousness. SPONSOR: --- Parallel is a single platform for all your agentic research: web search built for AI agents, with Pareto-optimal quality, cost and speed. Get started: https://parallel.ai/mlst?utm_source=creator&utm_medium=podcast&utm_content=MLST --- Bach's null hypothesis is that consciousness is easy: an algorithm not much more complicated than the transformer, simple enough for an infant's brain to discover by itself. In this conversation with Tim, he lays out the Machine Consciousness Hypothesis in two parts. The first is that consciousness is a biological learning algorithm, the training algorithm that makes a brain like ours coherent. The second is that machines learning in self-organising ways might discover it in the same way. Either part can fail on its own. From there they ask why there will never be a Turing test for consciousness, why a chess program is already a zombie, and why faking a mind can sometimes be harder than building one. The conversation runs through Leibniz's mill, the explanatory gap from John Searle to Thomas Nagel, Anil Seth's biological naturalism, integrated information theory and the letter that called it pseudoscience, Gödel and the limits of formal systems, and Mike Levin's idea that morphogenesis and the mind may run the same coherence algorithm. A tea-room interlude takes in Picbreeder and fractured, entangled representations. The episode closes on what it would take to convince us that a machine is conscious. --- TIMESTAMPS: 0:00 Cold open: Could consciousness be a learning algorithm? 1:51 Introduction 3:37 What makes an agent? 6:16 Why consciousness needs explaining 14:57 Sponsor: Parallel 15:51 Leibniz's mill and causal patterns 24:21 Perceiving that you perceive 32:04 Two hypotheses, two ways to fail 40:42 Do minds converge? 49:23 Does consciousness converge too? 56:20 When language models reshape our thinking 59:16 Can simulated water make you wet? 1:09:21 Computation as construction 1:16:03 Error-correcting patterns and the Ruliad 1:22:28 Conscious, or simulating consciousness? 1:28:23 What would count as evidence? 1:35:49 The research programme REFERENCES: Joscha Bach, The Machine Consciousness Hypothesis (California Institute for Machine Consciousness) Kumar, Clune, Lehman & Stanley, "Questioning Representational Optimism in Deep Learning: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis" Giulio Tononi, integrated information theory Fleming et al. 2023, "The Integrated Information Theory of Consciousness as Pseudoscience" John Searle 1980, "Minds, brains, and programs", Behavioral and Brain Sciences Kurt Gödel 1931, "On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems" Alan Turing 1950, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" Whitehead & Russell, Principia Mathematica Paul Thagard 2022, "Energy requirements undermine substrate independence and mind-body functionalism" Richard Sutton 2019, "The Bitter Lesson" Michael Graziano, attention schema theory Bernard Baars and Stanislas Dehaene, global workspace theory Michael Levin 2022, "Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere", Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience Chris Olah et al. 2020, "Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits", Distill Adele Lopez 2025, "The Rise of Parasitic AI", LessWrong RESCRIPT: https://app.rescript.info/share/fc7088df0dc8b84200aa6e01c9a9ab6a

title: Hacking Didn't Change. Its Price Did
summary: In episode 1040 of the SuperDataScience podcast, @JonKrohnLearns discusses with Amy Blackshaw, SVP at Palo Alto Networks, how the economics of cyberattacks have drastically changed due to frontier AI. Amy explains that while the attacks themselves haven't evolved, the cost of entry for attackers has plummeted, making enumeration free. The expensive part of an attack used to be the expert thinking, and frontier AI has made that instant, tireless and cheap. As Amy puts it, the villain is still the attacker, who now has the same capabilities defenders do.
